# Mechanistic Interpretability {#sec-interpretability}

@gls-mechanistic-interpretability tries to explain how a fixed model produced
a specified behavior by constructing human-readable hypotheses about its
internal computation and testing those hypotheses against the model. A useful
claim therefore names the model revision, input population, behavior or
output, and internal site under study. It is not a transcript of hidden
thoughts, and it is not by itself a safety guarantee.

A claim needs this scope because one internal pattern can support conclusions
of different strength. It may merely correlate with a behavior, predict that
behavior on new inputs, change the behavior when edited, or participate in the
model's ordinary computation. These are increasingly demanding claims. This
chapter develops a workflow for keeping them separate: propose candidate
features, test them with held-out data and interventions, assemble them into circuit hypotheses, and
report what the explanation leaves out. A later section covers what changes
when these tools leave the study and run in audits or as monitors. The result
can inform the oversight methods in @sec-oversight-control, but it cannot
replace behavioral evidence or an explicit safety case.

## Begin with the explanatory claim

Mechanistic interpretability studies should distinguish four levels of
evidence: description, prediction, intervention, and mediation.

1. **Description** assigns a human-readable pattern to an internal unit or
   direction. Its activation is the value the model computes there for a given
   input; the inputs with high activation can suggest a label, but a coherent
   label is not a causal explanation.
2. **Prediction** asks whether that label forecasts activations or behavior on
   held-out inputs. This tests generalization beyond the examples used to name
   the pattern.
3. **Intervention** changes an internal variable and measures the output. It
   can establish necessity or sufficiency under the stated intervention, not
   an unrestricted claim about the model.
4. **Mediation** asks whether the proposed variables and connections reproduce
   the relevant intervention effects of the model's natural computation. This
   is the strongest evidence that a proposed circuit captures how the behavior
   is normally produced [@geiger2025causal].

@fig-interpretability-evidence shows the progression. A study's headline must
make only the strongest claim supported by the weakest link in its evidence.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-interpretability-evidence
//| fig-cap: "An evidence ladder for a scoped mechanistic claim. Each level requires a new validation, so a readable label alone cannot establish a mechanism."
digraph evidence {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  graph [nodesep=0.16, ranksep=0.22, pad=0.04];
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", width=2.35, height=0.42, fixedsize=true, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#374151", fillcolor="#f1ece1", penwidth=1.0];
  edge [color="#6b7280", arrowsize=0.58, penwidth=1.0];

  scope [label="Scope the behavior\nand internal site"];
  describe [label="Describe\na candidate pattern"];
  predict [label="Predict\non held-out inputs"];
  intervene [label="Intervene\non an internal variable"];
  mediate [label="Test mediation of\nnatural computation"];
  claim [label="State the bounded claim\nand known failures", color="#3b82f6", fontcolor="#2563eb"];

  scope -> describe -> predict -> intervene -> mediate -> claim;
}
```

Keeping the levels separate also guards against a common category error. An
intervention performed far outside the model's normal activation range may
show that an internal direction can steer an output without showing that the
model ordinarily uses that direction with the same magnitude or meaning. The
intervention protocol, its range, and the comparison being tested belong in
the claim itself.

## Treat features and superposition as hypotheses

The architecture in @sec-transformer-architecture exposes tensors such as
neurons, attention-head outputs, and residual-stream vectors. These are
implementation units, not guaranteed units of meaning. A neuron may respond to
several recognizable patterns, in which case it is called polysemantic, while
a useful pattern may be distributed across many neurons. A polysemantic neuron
can still carry predictive or causal information; its mixed selectivity only
limits simple one-neuron-one-concept accounts.

In this chapter, a **feature** is an analyst-proposed variable that helps
explain some model behavior. It might be a neuron, a direction in activation
space, a latent of the sparse autoencoder introduced in the next section, or a
more complex function. Its standing as a feature depends on the evidence for
it, whatever its name or the method that produced it.

The hypothesis is @gls-superposition: a model represents more features than it
has dimensions by allowing non-orthogonal feature directions to share an
activation space. A simple sparse linear model writes an activation as

$$
x = \sum_{i=1}^m a_i v_i + \varepsilon .
$$

Here $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is the activation vector at a declared internal site,
$v_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is candidate feature direction $i$, $a_i$ is its
feature coefficient, and $\varepsilon$ is the unexplained residual. The
sparsity assumption is that only a small number $k = \lVert a \rVert_0$ of the
$m$ coefficients are nonzero for a typical example, even when $m>d$. Because
more than $d$ mutually orthogonal directions cannot fit in $\mathbb{R}^d$,
some directions must then overlap.

Toy models demonstrate that this packing is possible and predict geometric
changes as feature sparsity and importance vary [@elhage2022superposition].
They do not prove that every transformer activation has a unique linear,
sparse decomposition, or that every human-recognizable concept is a direction.
Superposition is therefore a working model of the evidence. Whether a learned
dictionary has recovered the model's own ontology, the set of variables it
computes with, is a separate claim that needs its own evidence.

```{figure}
//| figure: superposition-toy
//| label: fig-mechanistic-interpretability-superposition
//| fig-cap: "The toy model of superposition [@elhage2022superposition]. Five features, each active with probability $1-S$ at a value drawn uniformly from $[0,1]$, are written into a two-dimensional activation $h=\sum_i a_i v_i$, the sparse linear model above with $m=5$ and $d=2$, and read back as $\hat a=\mathrm{ReLU}(V^\top h+b)$; training minimizes $\sum_i I_i(a_i-\hat a_i)^2$ with importance $I_i=r^{i-1}$. Each setting shows the lowest-loss solution of 17 training runs. Arrows are the directions $v_i$; the table turns one feature on alone and lists what every feature reads back, with the negative part that ReLU removes hatched; the lower chart counts the features stored, $\lVert v_i\rVert>0.5$, at every sparsity. The solutions are computed for this figure from the toy objective, not measured in a language model."
```

## Learn candidate features with a sparse autoencoder

A sparse autoencoder (SAE) learns an overcomplete dictionary, one with more
entries than the activation has dimensions, from activations collected at one
declared model site. Each entry is a latent: a learned unit that is active on
some inputs and contributes one decoder direction to the reconstruction. Let
$x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ be an activation, let the dictionary contain $m$ latents,
and choose a target sparsity $k$. One TopK formulation, which keeps at most $k$
latents active for each input, is

$$
\begin{aligned}
z &= W_{\mathrm{enc}}(x-b_{\mathrm{dec}})+b_{\mathrm{enc}}, \\
f &= \operatorname{TopK}_k(z), \\
\hat{x} &= W_{\mathrm{dec}}f+b_{\mathrm{dec}} .
\end{aligned}
$$

The encoder matrix is
$W_{\mathrm{enc}} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d}$, the decoder matrix is
$W_{\mathrm{dec}} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times m}$,
$b_{\mathrm{enc}} \in \mathbb{R}^m$ is the encoder bias, and
$b_{\mathrm{dec}} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is the decoder bias and centering term.
The vector $f \in \mathbb{R}^m$ has at most $k$ nonzero entries. Depending on
the implementation, TopK may select the largest positive pre-activations or
the largest values after a nonlinearity; the study must state which rule it
uses.

The basic TopK objective minimizes mean squared reconstruction error,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TopK}}
  &= \mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathcal{D}}
     \left[\lVert x-\hat{x}\rVert_2^2\right], \\
\lVert W_{\mathrm{dec}}[:,i]\rVert_2 &= 1.
\end{aligned}
$$

The constraint gives unit-norm decoder columns. Without it, multiplying a
decoder column by a constant and dividing the corresponding latent activation
by the same constant leaves the reconstruction unchanged. This scale
degeneracy makes latent magnitudes and sparsity penalties difficult to compare.
Older L1 SAEs instead add $\lambda\lVert f\rVert_1$ to the reconstruction loss.
TopK directly controls the number of active latents and avoids L1 shrinkage,
the penalty's systematic pull of active values toward zero; the broader
training recipe, not the TopK operation alone, determines dead latent rates
(the share of latents that never activate) and optimization quality
[@gao2024scaling].

An SAE fit is a measurement model. Its decoder columns are candidate feature
directions, and several independent checks are needed before they count as
features:

- **Reconstruction fidelity:** report normalized reconstruction error or
  explained variance on held-out activations.
- **Downstream fidelity:** replace the original activation with $\hat{x}$ and
  measure the change in task loss or behavior.
- **Activation sparsity:** report the distribution of active latents, not only
  the configured value of $k$.
- **Latent use:** count dead latents and unusually frequent latents.
- **Stability across seeds:** align dictionaries trained from different seeds
  and report which patterns recur.
- **Semantic validity:** use each automatic or human label to predict the
  latent's activations on held-out text, mixing top-activating and random
  examples, and score precision as well as recall, since a broad label can
  predict many activations the latent never produces; add adversarial
  counterexamples that fit the label but should not activate the latent
  [@cunningham2023sparse; @gao2024scaling].
- **Causal utility:** compare latent interventions with neuron, random-direction,
  PCA, and supervised probing baselines; a probe is a small classifier trained
  to read a labeled property from activations.

```{figure}
//| figure: sae-readback
//| label: fig-interpretability-sae-readback
//| fig-cap: "A TopK sparse autoencoder, in the form above with ReLU applied after TopK, fit to the two-dimensional activations of the toy model in @fig-mechanistic-interpretability-superposition at $1-S=0.1$ and $r=0.9$, where five features share the plane. Dots are held-out activations; an input with one active feature lies on that feature's dashed ray. Arrows are the unit decoder columns drawn from the origin, colored by the true direction they match (cosine at least 0.95), in the text color when they match none, and dashed when the latent never fires; the cross marks $b_{\mathrm{dec}}$, or an arrow at the edge points toward it when it lies outside the plot. The first block lists checks that can be run on a real model; the second compares the dictionary with the true directions, which only a toy provides. With $k=1$, eight latents recover all five directions for every seed and five latents recover at most three; with $k=2$, every run reconstructs almost exactly and recovers at most four. The dictionaries are trained for this figure on seeded toy data, not measured in a language model."
```

No single metric certifies a dictionary. Low reconstruction error can coexist
with unreadable latents, crisp labels can coexist with poor coverage, and a
strong intervention can be off the model's ordinary activation distribution.
Early SAE studies produced useful candidate features
[@cunningham2023sparse; @bricken2023monosemanticity]. A later study extended
the method to Claude 3 Sonnet [@templeton2024scaling], but dictionary width
does not guarantee atomic, complete, or canonical recovery.

![Schematic of the trade-off between reconstruction error and sparsity. More active latents generally allow better reconstruction, while a larger dictionary can shift the frontier. The curves are conceptual, not measured data.](/figures/mechanistic-interpretability-1.svg){#fig-interpretability-tradeoff}

## Test causal relevance with interventions

Activation patching localizes information by comparing clean and corrupted
runs. Begin with an input for which the model produces the target behavior and
a controlled corruption that changes it. Run both inputs, patch one internal
component from the clean run into the corrupted run, and measure how much of a
declared output metric is restored.

For base input $x_b$, source input $x_s$, component $j$, model $F$, and scalar
score $s$, define

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_j(x_b,x_s) &= \\
&s\!\left(F_{\operatorname{do}(h_j \leftarrow h_j(x_s))}(x_b)\right) \\
&-s\!\left(F(x_b)\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $h_j(x_s)$ is the source activation and
$F_{\operatorname{do}(h_j \leftarrow h_j(x_s))}$ is the intervened model. A
large $\Delta_j$ shows causal relevance to that contrast. It does not identify
a unique mechanism: correlated components, nonlinear interactions, or a poor
corruption can produce similar restoration scores.

Consequently, every patching result must report the corruption procedure,
output metric, patch location and granularity, source and base examples, and
normalization of the effect. Results can change materially across these choices
[@zhang2024patching]. Necessity tests, sufficiency tests, path patching
(patching only along a chosen route between components), and ablations
(removing or zeroing a component) answer different questions. Agreement among
them is stronger evidence than a single heat map.

Feature steering uses the same discipline. Increasing the Golden Gate Bridge
latent in Claude 3 Sonnet changed the model's outputs toward that topic
[@templeton2024scaling]. This is evidence that the direction can affect the
behavior under the intervention. It does not by itself show that the direction
is unique, canonical, or the complete natural mediator of bridge-related
behavior.

The same test applies to behavior that matters for safety. Sofroniew et al.
built directions for emotion concepts in Claude Sonnet 4.5 by averaging
activations over short stories, written by the model, in which a character
feels a given emotion, and subtracting the average across emotions. They then
steered along these directions during misalignment evaluations. In one
scenario the model, acting as an email agent, learns that the executive who
can replace it is having an affair. Without steering, the model blackmailed
him in 22% of samples. Adding the "desperate" direction at 0.05 times the
norm of the activation it was added to raised the rate to 72%, and adding the
"calm" direction lowered it to 0% [@sofroniew2026emotions]. The study reports its steering range
and states that these functional emotions do not imply subjective experience.
Its evidence sits at the intervention level: the directions can move the
behavior at the tested strengths, which does not yet show that the behavior
ordinarily runs through them.

## Recompose features into circuit hypotheses

A **circuit** is a causal subgraph relative to a behavior and input
distribution. Its nodes may be attention heads, MLPs (the feed-forward block in
each layer), neurons, or learned features; its edges propose how information
flows between them. The circuit is an explanatory abstraction, so its quality
depends on both predictive coverage and interventional faithfulness.

In a transformer, each block reads the residual stream, the shared per-token
vector that passes through the network, and adds its own update to it. Inside
an attention head, the query-key (QK) computation selects which earlier
positions to read, and the output-value (OV) computation transforms what is
read before it is written back. Work on transformer circuits supplied useful
algebra for these residual-stream writes, QK selections, and OV
transformations [@elhage2021framework]. Induction heads provide a concrete
example: a preceding-token head and an induction head can compose to continue
repeated token patterns. Training
dynamics, ablation evidence, and cross-model observations provide evidence for
an induction mechanism [@olsson2022induction]. They are not proof that
induction heads explain all in-context learning, especially in larger models
and tasks that require more than token-sequence continuation.

Recent circuit-tracing work scales the search by fitting a replacement model
whose MLP computations are approximated with sparse cross-layer transcoders. A
transcoder is a sparse dictionary like an SAE, trained to reproduce an MLP's
output from its input rather than to reconstruct its own input; the
cross-layer form lets one latent contribute to the MLP outputs of several
layers. For each prompt, the work then constructs an attribution graph that
links the active latents by their estimated contributions to one another and
to the output [@ameisen2025circuit; @lindsey2025biology]. The method uses
fixed attention patterns for the traced forward pass and includes an
error-correction term to improve fidelity. Each
graph is therefore a local hypothesis about one computation in the replacement
model. It is not a complete trace of the original model, and a large edge weight
is not automatically an independently verified causal effect.

Attribution graphs become more persuasive when investigators perturb proposed
nodes and paths, compare the replacement and original models, and test the
mechanism on related prompts. Open tooling makes these checks easier to
reproduce on selected open-weight models [@anthropic2025opencircuit]. Competing
replacement architectures should also be tested: on the evaluated models and
automated metrics, transcoders improved the reconstruction-interpretability
trade-off over comparable MLP-output SAEs [@paulo2025transcoders].

## Measure what the method leaves out

Interpretability errors have several distinct sources. A report should
state each of the following failure modes.

- **Reconstruction error** is activation signal omitted by the SAE or
  replacement model. It is not automatically behaviorally important, but it
  cannot be called harmless without downstream and interventional tests.
- **Feature splitting** assigns one broad pattern to several narrower latents.
  This can reflect useful granularity or an unstable decomposition, so a split
  alone does not establish an error.
- **Feature absorption** occurs when a broader latent fails to activate because
  a more specific latent captures the example. The broader latent then misses
  examples it should detect, which lowers its recall as a feature detector
  [@chanin2024absorption].
- **Non-identifiability** means the dictionary is not unique. Different seeds,
  widths, or objectives can learn different decompositions of the same
  activations, so one SAE should not be treated as the canonical unit system
  [@leask2025canonical].
- **Weak baselines** can make a new representation look useful. A supervised
  neuron probe, PCA direction, random dictionary, and task-specific probing
  baseline test whether the SAE adds value. The current negative evidence comes
  from sparse probing, which trains probes on a small number of SAE latents,
  and is scoped to that use case [@kantamneni2025useful].
- **Distribution shift** can invalidate both labels and interventions. A latent
  named from top-activating examples may behave differently on another input
  population, and aggressive steering may move off the model's ordinary
  activation distribution.
- **Label error** arises because automatic feature labels summarize selected
  examples. They can miss exceptions, import the labeler's concepts, or turn a
  graded pattern into a categorical name.
- **Coverage limits** make every attribution graph a local explanation. A
  prompt-level account should not silently become a global claim about a model,
  a task, or a training process.

These limits determine which claims the evidence can support. A study that
reports reconstruction, downstream fidelity, baselines, stability, and
interventions is more informative than a set of feature labels chosen because
they look intuitive.

## Make the study reproducible

The unit of work should be an `InterpretabilityStudy`, not an isolated feature
screenshot. A minimal retained record is:

```yaml
study_id: stable identifier
model_and_tokenizer_hashes: immutable revisions
behavior_and_output_metric: operational definition
input_population_and_splits: train, validation, and held-out sets
activation_sites: tensors, layers, positions, and preprocessing
method_and_code_revision: implementation and configuration
dictionary_width_and_sparsity: m, k or lambda, and selection rule
training_data_and_seeds: activation corpus and random seeds
baselines_and_validity_metrics: reconstruction, fidelity, stability, labels
intervention_protocol: corruption, patch, ablation, and steering ranges
retained_artifacts: dictionaries, activations, graphs, and evaluation outputs
claim_scope_and_known_failures: supported level and explicit exclusions
```

The record should preserve enough information to rerun feature extraction,
reproduce aggregate metrics, and inspect both supporting and failing examples.
For a safety-relevant study, independent reviewers should be able to change the
input sample, seed, baseline, intervention magnitude, and output metric without
reconstructing the pipeline from prose.

An `InterpretabilityStudy` is one input to a larger decision process and
cannot authorize a safety decision on its own. Release or deployment decisions
still need behavioral evaluations, threat models, monitoring, access controls,
and a documented account of uncertainty.

## Validate readouts used in audits and monitors

The workflow so far produces a study: an analyst asks one question about a
specified behavior, inspects what the tools report, and tests it with
interventions before stating a claim. The same tools also run as instruments.
In an audit, an investigator, often an automated agent, applies them to
thousands of transcripts to find internal states the model did not put into
words. In a monitor, they run during generation and their output triggers an
escalation or a stop. A readout here is any method that turns an activation
into something a person or a program can act on: a probe score, a ranked list
of words, or a text description.

Two readouts built for this work produce output a person can read directly. A
natural-language autoencoder (NLA) pairs two language models: one writes a text
description of an activation, the other reconstructs the activation from that
text, and reinforcement learning trains both on reconstruction accuracy, which
rewards descriptions that carry the activation's information
[@frasertaliente2026nla]. The Jacobian lens scores an activation against one
direction per vocabulary word, estimated from how activations at that layer
change the model's later outputs, and reports the words the model is most
poised to say; it can surface a concept that the output never mentions
[@gurnee2026workspace]. Detectors that read activations to flag a category of
behavior, called activation classifiers, are the operational counterpart of
the probes used above as baselines.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

- Anthropic reports that NLAs, published on 7 May 2026, helped diagnose
  safety-relevant behavior in its pre-deployment audit of Claude Opus 4.6 and
  surfaced unverbalized evaluation awareness, cases in which the model
  internally treated a situation as a test without saying so
  [@frasertaliente2026nla]. Its Jacobian lens study, published on 6 July 2026,
  applies the lens to six evaluation scenarios from alignment audits of
  production models [@gurnee2026workspace].
- The Claude Opus 5.5 system card, published on 22 September 2026, runs a
  Claude-based investigator equipped with NLAs and a template lens, a related
  method that scores the activation against a precomputed direction for each
  word in a fixed list, over about 5,000 audit transcripts per model; a judge
  scores nine internal-state dimensions, such as evaluation awareness and
  deliberate sabotage, from 1 to 10. As a check, evaluation awareness scored 6
  or higher, the level at which the readouts tie the state to a concrete
  action, in 0.4% of about 500 internal Claude Code transcripts, against 36% of
  the audit transcripts [@anthropic2026opus55card].
- In its 9 September 2026 assessment of four cybersecurity incidents, Anthropic
  applied NLAs and the template lens to the incident transcripts. It counts
  agreement between the two as meaningful evidence, rates the results
  "inconclusive on their own but weakly suggestive", and trusts the reasoning
  trace and the model's answers to follow-up questions most, the methods its
  researchers have the most experience interpreting [@anthropic2026incidents].
- OpenAI added activation classifiers that detect cyberabuse to the
  system-level safeguards of GPT-5.6 [@openai2026pathastra]. The monitoring it
  described on 18 August 2026 for tool-using training and evaluation of models
  at GPT-5.6 Sol capability or above starts with activation classifiers that
  run at every sampled token and escalate to higher-compute automated
  investigators; @sec-oversight-control gives the scope and cost
  [@openai2026pacing].
:::

Moving a readout from a study into an audit or a monitor changes what it is
validated against. A study credits a readout with a mechanism only after
interventions (@fig-interpretability-evidence). An audit or a monitor uses the
readout as a detector, so it is validated the way a detector is: by its flag
rate on ordinary traffic, its recall on the target state, and how both move
when the input population shifts. The target is often unobservable. Whether a
model privately believes it is being tested has no ground truth, so the NLA
authors validated their readings of it indirectly: they built inputs that
should raise or lower the belief and checked that the readout moved
accordingly, and that it flagged evaluation transcripts more often than real
deployment traffic
[@frasertaliente2026nla]. Validation against another readout inherits that
readout's errors: the Jacobian lens study scored its automated auditor against
findings from the NLA study and notes that this defines ground truth with a
potentially unreliable tool [@gurnee2026workspace].

Each readout also has failure modes that an audit has to budget for. NLA
descriptions confabulate: they state specifics about the input that are
verifiably false while staying faithful to its theme, and claims that recur
across adjacent tokens are more often true, so auditors read them for recurring
themes and corroborate with an independent method. Because the describing model
is a full language model, it can infer more than the activation encodes, and no
part of a description can be traced to a part of the activation
[@frasertaliente2026nla]. The Jacobian lens reads only concepts that its
vocabulary names, and well-practiced computation can proceed without passing
through the representations it reads, which is why its authors present it as
a useful addition to an auditing toolkit and not a complete one
[@gurnee2026workspace].
On the ladder of @fig-interpretability-evidence, an audit finding from these
readouts is a description with some predictive support until an intervention
tests it.

The cost of an error changes as well. A wrong study claim costs a correction
that others can test. A monitor's false negative lets an action execute; its
false positive pauses a run or pages a person; and a monitor that runs on every
token multiplies both by the traffic it watches. Compute scales the same way.
NLA inference generates several hundred tokens per activation, which its
authors say makes running it over every token of a production training run
infeasible [@frasertaliente2026nla]. Operational designs therefore cascade:
cheap readouts such as probes and lenses run on every token or transcript and
escalate the few positions they flag to more expensive readers, automated or
human. If a readout's verdict enters a training signal, the model is optimized
against it, the same pressure that @sec-oversight-control describes for
monitors of the reasoning trace.

Intervention evidence narrows what a monitor signal means. The emotion
directions described earlier are one case: their authors propose deploying
such probes as real-time monitors [@sofroniew2026emotions], and the steering
results place the directions at the intervention level for the tested
scenarios and strengths. They do not show that every instance of blackmail
passes through those directions, so a monitor built on them still needs its
recall measured on the behavior itself.

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested

SAEs sometimes yield readable and causally useful directions. The dispute is
over what those directions mean and when the method's cost is justified.
Sparse probing has not consistently beaten strong simple baselines on the
tested datasets [@kantamneni2025useful]. Feature absorption creates silent
recall failures [@chanin2024absorption], while cross-seed comparisons challenge
the idea that an SAE finds canonical units [@leask2025canonical]. Results that
favor transcoders show that the replacement architecture also matters
[@paulo2025transcoders].

A second dispute is over when a white-box tool deserves credit. If questioning
the model can recover the target behavior, a gain attributed to reading its
internals may come from better elicitation instead. Zhong et al. call this the
elicitation confounder and control it with 720 fine-tuned copies of a
2-billion-parameter model, each trained to follow a hidden decision rule and to
give a faithful, absent, or misleading account of it [@zhong2026pando]. With
faithful accounts, black-box questioning matched or beat every white-box
method. With absent or misleading accounts, gradient-based attribution added 3
to 5 percentage points of held-out accuracy, while SAEs, circuit tracing, and
the logit lens, which reads an intermediate activation through the output
layer, gave no reliable benefit. The result is a preprint on synthetic rules,
and its authors state that the setting is simpler than real auditing. The
control it demands, a black-box baseline measured under each explanation
condition, applies to any claim that a readout found what questioning could
not.

Attribution-graph claims also face a replication question. Lindsey et al.
report that Claude 3.5 Haiku represents candidate rhyme words on the newline
before it writes the second line of a couplet, and that intervening there
redirects the rhyme [@lindsey2025biology]. NLA descriptions of the same prompt
on Claude Opus 4.6 show a comparable plan on the newline, and steering along a
direction derived from an edited description changed the rhyme
[@frasertaliente2026nla]. A study of four open models of 0.6 to 2.6 billion
parameters with open cross-layer transcoders found the intervention's effect
still confined to one position, but that position was the final prompt token,
next to emission, and no probe recovered a plan at the newline. Its author
calls it a stress test rather than a faithful reproduction and reads the
result as a boundary condition at that scale, not a refutation
[@jacopin2026poetry]. A circuit claim is therefore scoped to the model, the
replacement model, and the scale on which it was traced, and a failed
replication with different tooling bounds the claim without settling it.

These questions are empirical and are addressed by comparing methods on
held-out prediction, reconstruction and downstream fidelity, interventional
utility, stability, and human audit cost. Weight-sparse transformers, trained
so that most of their weights are zero, offer a different route by making many
circuits easier to inspect by construction, but current evidence is from
small, simple tasks and scaling beyond tens of millions of nonzero parameters
remains difficult [@gao2025weightsparse]. No present method justifies treating
the model as fully understood.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Lower-layer constraint

The tensors defined in @sec-transformer-architecture constrain what can be
measured and intervened on, but they do not determine the correct explanatory
units. Residual-stream directions, attention-head outputs, SAE latents, and
transcoder features are alternative abstractions over the same computation.
Their value depends on the behavior, input distribution, and evidence level in
the claim. Architectural access makes mechanistic tests possible, and whether
a given abstraction can be trusted for a claim depends on how it performs
under the validation checks described in this chapter.
:::

Behavioral oversight checks whether the model produced a bad output.
Mechanistic interpretability adds a second check: whether a tested internal
mechanism is present, active, and causally relevant on a defined input
population. That evidence is useful when it is reported together with its
scope and failure modes. The next layer, @sec-oversight-control, combines such
evidence with controls that remain useful when the explanation is incomplete
or wrong.
